card: Transfers ownership of BlockManager out of ChainstateManager into NodeContext and the bitcoinkernel wrapper, passing BlockManager into ChainstateManager by reference. Currently, block storage cannot exist independently of chainstate management, which prevents kernel callers from inspecting or pruning block directories without running chainstate verification. The change also removes the redundant ChainstateLoadOptions::prune flag in favor of querying BlockManager directly. This addresses kernel limitations discussed in issue #35627 and unblocks PR #36854 and PR #36856.
changed_since_previous: Dropped the encapsulation refactors (RequestPrune, MarkBlockIndexDirty, removing BlockManager friend classes) and the movement of ImportBlocks to node/chainstate; those are deferred to #36858. Also dropped the dependency on #36738.
evidence: Author description cites issue #35627 ('kernel: can't work with pruned blocksdir') as motivation for moving block storage ownership out of ChainstateManager.
Author states that without removing the redundant prune flag, 'Once the kernel can prune (#36856), that would make it refuse to reopen a data directory it had pruned.'
problem: ChainstateManager creates and owns BlockManager, meaning block storage cannot exist or be configured, inspected, or pruned independently of full chainstate management. This blocks kernel callers from handling block storage or operating on pruned data directories on their own.

risk.why: Incorrect object lifetimes between BlockManager and ChainstateManager could cause use-after-free crashes during node shutdown or initialization failure.

summary: Transfers ownership of BlockManager out of ChainstateManager into NodeContext and the kernel's ChainMan wrapper, passing BlockManager to ChainstateManager by reference. ChainstateManager is explicitly destroyed before BlockManager to preserve teardown order. It also eliminates the redundant ChainstateLoadOptions::prune flag in favor of querying BlockManager directly.
